summary: Defines an authorization policy language for controlling access to location information. It extends the Common Policy framework with condition elements specific to location, so people can say who may see where they are. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: It is like a privacy rule list for your location, deciding who can know where you are and who cannot.

questions: how to control who can see my location
subtitle: A rule language that lets people say who may see their location, and how precisely.

tldr.problem: Location information is sensitive, and the basic privacy flags that travel with a location object can only convey preferences. They do not control who gets access or how precise the answer is.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC extends the Common Policy rule framework with location-specific conditions, such as being inside a circle or at a given civic address, and with transformations that set retention and retransmission flags and reduce the granularity of the location returned.
tldr.outcome: A Location Server can evaluate these XML rules and hand each requester a possibly blurred location. The RFC itself warns that its two obfuscation algorithms are examples with real limits.

facts.label: Civic levels
facts.value: country, region, city, building, full (default none)

today: RFC 6772 is a Proposed Standard from January 2013, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It extends RFC 4745, and the RFC itself notes that more algorithms may be needed for applications with stricter privacy requirements.

sections.title: Why Location Needs a Policy Language
sections.content:
RFC 6772 defines an authorization policy language for controlling access to location information. It builds on the model in RFC 6280, where a Location Generator determines location, a Location Server (LS) decides who may see it, a Location Recipient (LR) asks for it, and a Rule Maker (RM) writes the rules.

The basic rule set carried in a PIDF-LO location object (RFC 4119) can limit how long a recipient keeps the data and can forbid passing it on. But it does not protect access; it only conveys the user's wishes. The enhanced rule set in this RFC lets a Rule Maker restrict retention, deny particular people, restrict by time or by where the Target is, and reduce the resolution of what is returned.

The document does not describe the protocol that carries location from the Location Server to the Location Recipient.
sections.plainLanguage: A note that says please do not share my address is only a polite request. This RFC adds a real guard at the door who checks a list before telling anyone where you are.

sections.title: Rules, Permissions and Transport
sections.content:
The RFC extends the Common Policy framework of RFC 4745. A rule set is an unordered list of rules, and each rule has conditions, actions and transformations. Actions and transformations together are called permissions. The document is XML and keeps the Common Policy media type, application/auth-policy+xml.

Every permission is a positive grant of information. Because of that, combining permissions from several sources is well defined, and the lack of any action or transformation can only result in less information reaching the recipient.

Rules can travel in two ways. A PIDF-LO can point to enhanced rules by URL in its ruleset-reference element. Rules can also be stored at a Location Server or Presence Server and managed by the Rule Maker with XCAP (RFC 4825). When several rules match a request, the combined permission is evaluated as described in Section 10 of RFC 4745.
sections.plainLanguage: Each rule is an if-then card: if the person asking looks like this, then show them this much. Cards only ever add things people may see, so a missing card means they see less, never more.

sections.title: Location Conditions
sections.content:
A rule's <conditions> element can hold <location-condition> children, which must each contain at least one <location> element. The condition is true if any child <location> matches the Target's location (a logical OR). A <location> has three attributes: profile, xml:lang and label, the last being a human-readable description.

Two profiles exist. The geodetic profile (geodetic-condition) uses a GML circle and is true when the Target's current location is completely within it. Implementations MUST support WGS 84 in two dimensions, identified as urn:ogc:def:crs:EPSG::4326, and the CRS must be given with the srsName attribute. If the geodetic location is unknown, the condition is false.

The civic profile (civic-condition) uses a <civicAddress> element from RFC 5139. Every child element must match the Target's civic location by octet-by-octet comparison (a logical AND). If no civic address is present, the condition is false, and a Location Server is RECOMMENDED not to geocode a geodetic location into a civic one.

If a rule evaluator does not understand an extension, the rule evaluates to false.
sections.plainLanguage: A rule can say only if I am inside this circle on the map, or only if I am at this exact street address. If the guard cannot tell where you are, or does not understand the rule, the rule does not fire.

sections.title: Transformations
sections.content:
The RFC defines no location-specific actions. It defines transformations, which change what the Location Server returns. Four of them set the basic rules inside the PIDF-LO:

  • set-retransmission-allowed: a boolean that sets retransmission-allowed. If absent, the value is unchanged, or FALSE for a newly created PIDF-LO.
  • set-retention-expiry: a non-negative number of seconds added to the time the LS provides location. Zero requests that the information is not retained.
  • set-note-well: a human-readable privacy statement with an xml:lang attribute.
  • keep-rule-reference: whether the external-ruleset reference stays in the PIDF-LO. If FALSE, the reference is removed and no rules are carried as MIME bodies.

The fifth, provide-location, controls granularity. With no children, civic and geodetic location are disclosed without reduction, subject to availability, and the profile attribute MUST NOT be present. With children, profile MUST be present: civic-transformation for a provide-civic child, or geodetic-transformation for a provide-geo child.

The civic levels are country, region, city, building and full, each including everything in the lower ones; the default is none. The geodetic profile uses a radius attribute in meters and refers only to WGS 84.
sections.plainLanguage: Transformations are the dials on what you reveal. One dial says how long the other person may remember it, one says whether they may tell others, and one blurs your spot from your exact room down to just your country.

sections.title: The Geodetic Obfuscation Algorithm
sections.content:
To blur a geodetic position, the RFC gives a six-step grid algorithm. Steps 1 and 2 are done once per region and desired uncertainty: choose a map projection whose distortion MUST be below 1.5, then lay out a grid of landmarks at least distance d apart, where d is the desired uncertainty radius.

For each measured position, find the four landmarks around it, compute its scaled local coordinates x and y inside that grid square, and compare them to p = 0.2887 and q = 0.7113. This sorts the position into one of eight cases, each of which names one or two candidate corners. The result is a circle with that corner as center and radius d.

Because the grid is fixed, the same area is reported while the Target stays in the same place, which stops a recipient from averaging many random answers into a precise fix. Section 7.5 works the algorithm through for a point near Denver with d of 100 km, and shows how grids for different latitude bands keep distortion low.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine the map covered by a big checkerboard of landmarks. Instead of saying exactly where you are, the guard names a nearby landmark and a circle around it, and keeps naming the same one while you stay put.

sections.title: Limits of Hiding Location
sections.content:
The RFC is frank that obfuscation is hard. An obscured location is still true: the Location Server hides the Target inside a larger shape rather than lying. Returning randomly computed shapes would reveal more over time, which is why the grid algorithm gives the same answer in the same area. Even so, new answers when the Target moves reveal movement, and a Target who regularly visits the same place can be analyzed.

Civic reduction leaks too: at building level, moving from one building to the next is still visible. Public geographic information such as highways or lakes can narrow things down further. For the grid algorithm, the RFC states that the observed region A1 relative to the privacy-region area A stays above 0.13.

Further cautions: users may write policies where a small movement flips what is disclosed, so policy-authoring software should check consistency. Selectively withholding data reveals that something is worth hiding. The RFC concludes that obscuring is unlikely to stop a determined adversary and that withholding location entirely is perhaps the most effective method.
sections.plainLanguage: Blurring a photo helps, but someone who sees many blurry photos over time, or who knows the neighborhood, can often guess the answer. Sometimes the safest thing is to show nothing at all.

sections.title: XCAP Usage and Registrations
sections.content:
For managing rules over XCAP, the RFC registers the Application Unique ID geolocation-policy. The default namespace is urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:geolocation-policy, and documents live under a user path of the form http://[xcaproot]/geolocation-policy/users/foo. By default only a user can read, write or modify their own documents.

IANA also receives two XML schema registrations, two namespace registrations, and a new registry of location profile names run under Specification Required. The initial names are geodetic-condition, civic-condition, geodetic-transformation and civic-transformation, so new obfuscation algorithms can be added later.

Implementations MUST understand UTF-8 and UTF-16 and MUST NOT encode these XML documents with any other encoding.
sections.plainLanguage: This part files the paperwork: it gives the rulebook an official name and a place in the filing cabinet, and leaves room to add new kinds of blurring later.

items.label: No civic data
items.desc: The default value; nothing is disclosed.

items.label: Building
items.desc: Adds street and house number data but hides floor, room and similar internal detail.

items.label: Full
items.desc: Adds the remaining civic items, such as floor, room and unit.
